results.title: UK PMI  -  acute vs chronic definition, coverage stops

verdict.headline: This policy stops paying for chronic conditions after 12 months, leaving you reliant on the NHS for ongoing care.
verdict.summary: The most significant issue is a hard 12-month benefit cap on all chronic conditions â after which coverage ends entirely for that condition, including monitoring and medication. The definition of 'chronic condition' is extremely broad and would capture many common long-term illnesses. Once the cap is hit, you bear the full cost privately or must return to NHS waiting lists. There are no other clauses visible in the provided text, so this analysis is limited to what was supplied.

topFindings.title: Chronic condition coverage cuts off completely after 12 months
topFindings.shortWhy: The policy explicitly states 'no further benefits will be payable for that condition' once 12 months of claims have passed â meaning a condition diagnosed and first claimed in year one receives zero cover from year two onwards.

topFindings.title: The definition of 'chronic condition' is wide enough to catch many everyday illnesses
topFindings.shortWhy: The definition includes any condition that 'comes back or is likely to come back' or 'needs ongoing or long-term control or relief of symptoms' â language broad enough to cover asthma, diabetes, depression, recurring back pain, migraines, and many other common conditions.

topFindings.title: Monitoring, maintenance medication, and management are explicitly excluded after 12 months
topFindings.shortWhy: The policy specifically names 'ongoing monitoring, maintenance medication, and management' as excluded after the 12-month window â so even low-cost, routine care for a chronic condition receives no contribution after that point.

clauseCards.originalTextExcerpt: We will pay for eligible treatment of a chronic condition for a maximum period of 12 months from the date we first pay a benefit for that condition. After this 12-month period, no further benefits will be payable for that condition under this policy, and you will need to seek treatment through the NHS.
clauseCards.atFirstGlance: It sounds like the policy covers chronic conditions, just with a time limit â reasonable enough for a private health plan.
clauseCards.whatItMeans: Coverage for a chronic condition does not taper down or reduce â it stops entirely after 12 months. From month 13 onwards, every consultation, test, prescription, and hospital visit related to that condition is either paid by you out of pocket or handled through the NHS. If you have a condition that requires years of management â which is the nature of most chronic conditions â this policy effectively provides only a one-year window of private cover before withdrawing completely.
clauseCards.scenario: You are diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes in March 2025. The insurer pays your first benefit claim that month, starting the 12-month clock. By March 2026, your endocrinologist appointments, blood tests, and medication reviews are no longer covered. You either pay privately â potentially hundreds of pounds per appointment â or join an NHS waiting list for ongoing diabetic management.
whatToDo: Before signing: Ask the insurer for a written list of conditions they have previously classified as chronic, so you know which of your existing or likely future health needs fall outside long-term cover.
Before signing: If you have any pre-existing or recurring condition, assume it will be classified as chronic and calculate whether one year of private cover is worth the premium cost for you.

Before signing: Compare this policy against alternatives that offer longer or uncapped chronic condition cover â some UK private health insurers offer continued cover for chronic conditions with different terms.
If a claim is made: Note the exact date the insurer first pays a benefit for any condition, as this starts the 12-month clock. Keep a written record.
Ongoing: If you reach month 10 of a chronic condition claim, contact your GP to begin any NHS referrals you may need, as NHS waiting times mean you should not wait until cover ends.
clauseCards.goDeeper: The 12-month period runs from the date the insurer first pays a benefit â not from your diagnosis date or the date you first sought treatment. This means the clock could start earlier than you expect if you make an initial claim quickly after symptoms appear.
risks: A condition you assumed would be covered long-term is cut off after one year, leaving you with ongoing private costs or NHS waiting times.

The policy does not appear to offer any transition support, partial cover, or appeal route once the 12-month cap is reached â though the full policy wording should be checked for any such provisions.

clauseCards.originalTextExcerpt: Chronic condition means a disease, illness, or injury that has one or more of the following characteristics: (a) it needs ongoing or long-term monitoring through consultations, examinations, check-ups, and/or tests; (b) it needs ongoing or long-term control or relief of symptoms; (c) it requires your rehabilitation or for you to be specially trained to cope with it; (d) it continues indefinitely; (e) it has no known cure; (f) it comes back or is likely to come back.
clauseCards.atFirstGlance: This looks like a standard medical definition â chronic conditions are serious, long-term illnesses like cancer or heart disease.
clauseCards.whatItMeans: Only one of the six listed characteristics needs to apply for a condition to be classified as chronic. Characteristic (f) â 'comes back or is likely to come back' â is particularly wide. A recurring sports injury, seasonal allergies, recurring urinary tract infections, or a second episode of depression could all qualify. Characteristic (b) â 'needs ongoing or long-term control or relief of symptoms' â could capture asthma, migraines, or anxiety managed with medication. The insurer, not you, determines whether a condition meets this definition, and the bar is low.
clauseCards.scenario: You suffer a second episode of lower back pain 18 months after the first. The insurer classifies it as a chronic condition under characteristic (f) because it 'came back.' Your physiotherapy and MRI scan are covered for 12 months from the first benefit payment, but if the condition persists or recurs again, no further cover is available under this policy.
whatToDo: Before signing: Ask the insurer directly whether specific conditions relevant to your health history â including any past recurring illnesses â would be classified as chronic under this definition.
Before signing: Ask whether a condition that recurs after a gap of several years would be treated as a new acute condition or as the same chronic condition.
Before a claim: If you are unsure whether a condition will be classified as acute or chronic, ask the insurer in writing before treatment begins, so you can plan accordingly.
If a claim is denied or reclassified: Request the insurer's written reasoning and check whether their classification matches the definition in the policy wording.
clauseCards.goDeeper: The definition of 'acute condition' requires that the condition 'is likely to respond quickly to treatment' and lead to 'full recovery.' If your condition does not result in full recovery â even if it is not severe â it may fall outside the acute definition and into the chronic category by default.
risks: Conditions you consider minor or one-off may be classified as chronic if they recur, triggering the 12-month cap sooner than expected.
The insurer has broad discretion to apply this definition, and the policy text does not describe a clear challenge or appeal process for disputed classifications.

clauseCards.clauseLabel: Explicit Exclusion of Monitoring, Medication, and Management After 12 Months
clauseCards.originalTextExcerpt: Ongoing monitoring, maintenance medication, and management of chronic conditions beyond the 12-month period are excluded.
clauseCards.atFirstGlance: This seems like a natural consequence of the 12-month cap â once cover ends, it ends.
clauseCards.whatItMeans: This sentence goes further than simply ending cover â it specifically names the three types of care most commonly needed for chronic conditions: monitoring (check-ups, blood tests, scans), maintenance medication (repeat prescriptions, drug reviews), and management (specialist consultations, care plans). By naming these explicitly, the policy removes any ambiguity that might otherwise allow you to argue that routine follow-up care is a separate, new acute episode. After 12 months, these are categorically excluded.
clauseCards.scenario: You are treated for an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) and the insurer pays benefits for 12 months. After that, your annual blood tests to check thyroid levels, your endocrinologist review appointments, and any medication adjustments are all excluded. These are not expensive individually, but over years they add up â and if you want to remain in private care, you pay in full.
whatToDo: Before signing: Estimate the likely annual cost of monitoring and medication for any chronic condition you have or are at risk of developing, and compare that to what you would pay out of pocket after the 12-month window closes.
Before a claim: Ask your specialist at the outset how long active treatment is likely to last versus how long ongoing monitoring will be needed â this helps you plan for when the cap will bite.
Ongoing: Keep records of all benefit payments and dates so you can track when the 12-month window is approaching for any given condition.
If approaching the 12-month limit: Ask your GP to take over monitoring and prescribing through the NHS before private cover ends, to avoid a gap in care.
clauseCards.goDeeper: Maintenance medication is explicitly excluded after 12 months. If your chronic condition requires ongoing prescription drugs that are not available on the NHS, or where NHS waiting times for a prescription review are long, this exclusion could have a direct impact on your treatment continuity.
risks: Routine but essential care â blood tests, annual specialist reviews, repeat prescriptions â becomes entirely self-funded after the 12-month cap.
There is no partial cover or reduced benefit after the cap; the exclusion is total.

recommendedQuestions: If a condition I had several years ago recurs, will it be treated as a new acute condition or as the same chronic condition subject to the 12-month cap?
Can you give me examples of conditions you have previously classified as chronic under the 'comes back or is likely to come back' characteristic?
What is the process for disputing a decision that my condition has been classified as chronic rather than acute?
Does the 12-month clock reset if I switch to a new policy year, or does it run continuously from the date of first benefit payment regardless of renewal?
Are there any add-on options or upgraded plan tiers that provide longer or uncapped cover for chronic conditions?

letterTemplates.title: Request for Written Confirmation of Chronic Condition Classification and Cover Period
letterTemplates.body:
Dear Member Services,

I am writing to request written confirmation of how my policy applies to chronic conditions before I proceed with treatment.

I understand from the policy wording that cover for a chronic condition is limited to a maximum of 12 months from the date you first pay a benefit for that condition, after which 'no further benefits will be payable for that condition under this policy.' I also note that 'ongoing monitoring, maintenance medication, and management' are explicitly excluded after this period.

I would be grateful if you could confirm in writing:

1. Whether [condition name, if applicable] would be classified as a chronic condition under your policy definition â specifically, which of the six listed characteristics you consider to apply.
2. The exact date from which the 12-month benefit period would run for this condition.
3. What the process is for challenging a classification decision if I believe a condition has been incorrectly categorised as chronic.
4. Whether any cover options exist beyond the 12-month period, including any upgrades or add-ons to my current plan.

Please respond in writing so I have a clear record of the cover available to me before I commit to a course of treatment.

Yours sincerely,
[Your name]
[Policy number]

letterTemplates.title: Formal Appeal Against Classification of [Condition] as a Chronic Condition
letterTemplates.body:
Dear Claims Team,

I am writing to formally appeal the decision to classify [condition name] as a chronic condition under my policy.

Your policy defines a chronic condition as one that has one or more of a list of characteristics, including that it 'comes back or is likely to come back' or 'needs ongoing or long-term control or relief of symptoms.' I do not believe my condition meets this threshold because [insert your reasons â e.g. my treating clinician has confirmed this is an acute episode with an expected full recovery, or this is a first occurrence with no expectation of recurrence].

As a result of this classification, I have been informed that my cover will end 12 months from the date of first benefit payment, and that monitoring, medication, and management will be excluded thereafter. I believe this classification is incorrect and is causing me material financial harm.

I request that you:
1. Review the classification decision in light of the clinical evidence I am providing.
2. Confirm in writing the outcome of this review and the reasons for your decision.
3. Advise me of any further escalation or independent review options available if my appeal is unsuccessful.

I am happy to provide supporting documentation from my treating clinician if required.

Yours sincerely,
[Your name]
[Policy number]
[Date of original decision]
